newsitem.title: USA: PaineWebber prefers to stay independent.
newsitem.headline: PaineWebber prefers to stay independent.

text.p: NEW YORK, April 16 (Reuter) PaineWebber Group Inc prefers to stay out of the way of the current merger wave in financial services and steer an independent course, chairman and chief executive Donald Marron said Wednesday.
"We think being an independent full-service firm is the way to go for us," Marron said in response to a reporter's question after a talk at the Baruch Business Forum sponsored by Baruch College here.

Asked if he agreed with a comment Tuesday by Merrill Lynch and Co Inc's new chairman and chief executive David Komansky that there was "an unfair playing field" between banks and securities firms in the merger arena, Marron said Komansky was "absolutely right."
"At the present moment you have a situation where a bank can buy someone in our business and we can't buy a bank," he continued. "It's completely unfair."

In his remarks to the breakfast meeting, Marron said the financial services industry has been transformed by the accumulation of huge sums of money in defined contribution retirement plans (in which individuals--rather than their corporate employers -- make their own investment decisions).

He said this situation presents several problems. He said some indivudals are saving too little or not at all and will not be prepared for retirement. Others will invest too conservatively and have too little.

He also said some people may get the wrong impression that the money in their defined contribution retirement plans belongs entirely to them. He said the truth is that 30 to 40 percent belongs to the government. "It will go to one taxing agency or another" when withdrawn from the retirement account, he said.

Marron said the growth of defined contribution retirement plans creates a demand for investment advice. In response to a question, he said while the Internet is a communications medium with investment advice and can also be a transaction medium, at the same time the Net made provide "too much information" for laypersons to use effectively.
